t.2.111.1: But Anasūyā, knower of dharma, having heard that great tale, embraced Maithilī with both arms and kissed her on the head.
t.2.111.2: What you have spoken is charming and sweet, its syllables and words clearly uttered; how the svayaṃvara took place, all of that I have indeed heard.
t.2.111.4: The cry is heard of the birds that scattered all day in search of food and now, at the hour of twilight, have settled down to sleep.
t.2.111.3: I am deeply delighted by your story, O sweet-spoken one. The glorious sun has gone to its setting, bringing on the auspicious night.
t.2.111.6: When the agnihotra offerings of the sages have been poured according to the prescribed rites, smoke, reddish like the body of a dove, is seen stirred up by the wind.
t.2.111.5: And these sages too, still wet from their ritual bath and washing their fruits, are coming here together, their bark garments drenched with water.
t.2.111.8: Creatures that roam by night are moving about on every side, for these deer of the hermitage forest lie down to rest at the sacred places by the altars.
t.2.111.7: For the trees, though scant of leaf, have grown dense on every side, such trees that even in a far-off region the directions do not shine clearly.
t.2.111.9: Night has come on, O Sītā, adorned with stars; the moon, cloaked in moonlight, is seen risen in the sky.
t.2.111.10: You may go; I give you leave. Be the companion of Rāma, for I have been well pleased by you as you spoke so sweetly.
t.2.111.11: Now adorn yourself, Maithilī, here before my eyes; dear child, resplendent with these celestial ornaments, give me joy.
t.2.111.12: Then Sītā, like a daughter of the gods, having adorned herself, bowed her head to her and went toward Rāma.
t.2.111.13: Rāghava, the best of speakers, saw Sītā thus adorned, and he rejoiced at the loving gift of the female ascetic.
t.2.111.14: Then Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, told Rāma everything about the loving gift of garments, ornaments and garlands given by the ascetic woman.
t.2.111.15: Rāma was overjoyed, and so was Lakṣmaṇa, the great chariot-warrior, on seeing the honor shown to Maithilī, an honor most rare among human beings.
t.2.111.16: Then the delight of the Raghus, his face like the moon, spent that holy night there in contentment, honored by the ascetics and the Siddhas.
t.2.111.17: When that night had passed, the two tigers among men, having bathed, took leave of the forest-dwelling ascetics, who had already made their offerings into the sacred fire.
t.2.111.19: This is the path of the great sages who gather fruits in the forest; by this way, O Rāghava, it is fitting for you to go into the impassable forest.
t.2.111.18: Those forest-dwelling ascetics, who lived by dharma, told the two of them that the paths of that forest were overrun by rākṣasas.
t.2.111.20: Thus blessed for a safe journey by those ascetic brahmins with folded hands, Rāghava, scorcher of foes, together with his wife and with Lakṣmaṇa, entered the forest, as the sun enters a bank of clouds.
